title: Plain Scones
subtitle: Light, tall scones for cream tea
excerpt: The key to a well-risen scone is cold butter, a hot oven, and no overworking. These bake in under 15 minutes and are best eaten the same day, split and spread generously.
sourceNotes: Scones are a cornerstone of the British cream tea tradition, with strong regional associations in Devon and Cornwall. The debate over whether to apply cream or jam first is firmly a matter of county loyalty.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked scones on the day they are made. Reheat from frozen at 180C for 8 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple easily. Freeze surplus to reheat on demand.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten fresh. They stale quickly after 24 hours.

content.text: Handle the dough as little as possible. Every extra fold toughens the scone and stops it rising.

items.prepNote: plus a little extra to brush

content.text: Heat the oven to 220C. Dust a baking tray with flour.
Put the flour in a large bowl. Add the butter. Rub together quickly until the mix looks like breadcrumbs.
Pour in the milk. Stir with a round-bladed knife until the dough just comes together.
Tip onto a lightly floured surface. Pat out to about 2.5cm thick. Do not roll.
Cut out rounds with a 6cm cutter. Press straight down. Do not twist the cutter.
Place on the tray. Brush the tops with beaten egg.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until well risen and golden brown.
Cool on a wire rack. Serve warm.

items.cause: Cutter was twisted, sealing the edges and stopping the rise.
items.fix: Press the cutter straight down, then lift without twisting.

items.cause: Too much flour worked in, or dough was overhandled.
items.fix: Use a light touch. Stop mixing the moment the dough holds together.

items.cause: Dough was too wet or oven not hot enough.
items.fix: Measure milk carefully. Preheat the oven fully before baking.
